anaerobic degradation of organics, while N2O is produced as the result of the biological removal of nitrogen (N) through enhanced nitriﬁcation and denitriﬁcation (e.g. Kampschreur et al., 2009; Law et al., 2012; Shaw and Koh, 2011). In order to formulate effective mitigation strategies against global climate change, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) formulated a guideline in 2006 to account for GHG emissions under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The guideline considers that carbon in wastewater to be biogenic, and thus on-site emis- sions of CO2 are to be excluded from reporting, while CH4 and N2O emissions from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) are included in the national inventory ([Bogner](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [2007)](#acknowledgments). In addition, N2O is now listed as the leading ozone depletion substance (Ravishankara et al., 2009). For the past 15 years, measurement campaigns have been conducted to determine reliable emission factors from WWTPs. A wide range of emission rates have been reported for N2O at WWTPs. Be- tween 0.001 and 2.59% of the N in the inﬂuent has reportedly been emitted as N2O by WWTPs operating biological nitrogen removal processes ([Benckiser](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [1996;](#acknowledgments) [Ahn](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [2010)](#acknowledgments). An even higher emission rate was reported by a plant equipped with sequencing N removal batch reactors (5.6% of N in inﬂuent; Sun et al., 2013) and a plant with the combination of partial nitriﬁcation and anammox process (5.1e6.6% of N in inﬂuent; Desloover et al., 2011).

Spot emission measurements using ﬂoating ﬂux cham- bers, combined with an analysis of liquid samples have been the most prevalent way of measuring fugitive GHG emissions from WWTPs ([Czepiel](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [1995;](#acknowledgments) [Su¨](#acknowledgments) [mer](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [1995;](#acknowledgments) [Sommer](#acknowledgments)

[et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [1998;](#acknowledgments) [Foley](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [2010;](#acknowledgments) [Ren](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [2012;](#acknowledgments) [Aboobarkar](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [2013)](#acknowledgments). While several studies have been conducted over extended time periods (e.g. one year (Su¨ mer et al., 1995) and one-and-a-half years for (Sommer et al., 1998), the results of the measurements provide only a snapshot of these dynamic systems and may not fully capture changes in emissions over time (Daelman et al., 2013a). In a few cases, in-line continuous measurements have been performed at WWTPs equipped with extensive air collection systems (Daelman et al., 2013b, 2012; Toyoda et al., 2011). Although these measurements provide an extensive dataset and are able to capture diurnal and seasonal changes in emissions, they only cover a portion of the plant, and so physical GHG leakages from pipes and ﬁttings, as well as incidental releases of gases outside of the ventilation system, are not captured.

Besides spot and in-line measurements, some attempts have been made to quantify whole plant-scale GHG emissions escaping from open WWTPs. Recently Yver-Kwok et al. (submitted for publication), compared regional and plant- integrated measurement technologies for CH4 emissions with the ﬂoating chamber methods, conﬁrming the efﬁcacy of the plant-integrated method. Modrak et al. (2006) applied a vertical radial plume mapping method using an open-path Fourier transform infrared (OP-FTIR) instrumentation. They found elevated concentrations of CH4 and N2O but were only able to quantify the CH4 emission rate due to the background concentration of N2O and the limited sensitivity of the in- strument. In order to overcome these limitations, and to provide reliable plant-integrated GHG emissions measure- ments for wastewater and sludge treatment processes, a

tracer dispersion method was used in this study by employing instrumentation optimized specially for measuring small CH4 and N2O concentration changes. The measurements were performed by recording downwind gas concentrations with a mobile cavity ring-down spectroscopy (CRDS) sampling de- vice, and dilution factors were calculated through the use of a tracer gas. The design of the instrument enables accurate measurements of trace gases in parts per trillion levels and has been used for analytically-demanding challenges such as measuring stable isotopes in ice cores (Dahl-Jensen et al., 2013). This method enables the real-time quantiﬁcation of total GHG emissions from the target facility over extended time and space. The same method has been applied at waste management facilities with high spatial and temporal het- erogeneity in GHG emissions, such as landﬁlls and compost- ing plants ([Andersen](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [2009;](#acknowledgments) [Scheutz](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [2011;](#acknowledgments) [Mønster](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [2012,](#acknowledgments) [in](#acknowledgments) [press)](#acknowledgments).

The measurement campaign was conducted at a municipal WWTP operating a biological nitrogen removal process and anaerobic digestion for sludge stabilization. Attempts were made to correlate operational conditions to the rate of GHG emissions. Finally, the measured emissions were compared against emission factors reported by previous studies. To the best of the author's knowledge, this is the ﬁrst time that the plant-integrated emissions measurement of N2O from a WWTP has been conducted using the tracer dispersion method.

2\. Methodology

2.1. Site description

The Avedøre Wastewater Treatment Plant (AV WWTP) is located southwest of Copenhagen, Denmark. Annually, it treats 25.3 million m3 of wastewater, which is generated by 265,000 inhabitants. Fig. 1 presents an aerial photo of the fa- cility. The AV WWTP accepts urban runoff water and is equipped with a ﬂow equalization basin to reduce ﬂuctuations in incoming wastewater volumes (1). Once entering the plant, wastewater is subjected to preliminary treatment whereby large objects and sand are removed (2). It is then sent to sedimentation basins, where relatively heavy solids are settled out and primary sludge is generated (3).Finally, efﬂuent from the primary sedimentation basins is sent to a secondary BioDeNitro conﬁguration treatment process, which consists of two reactors with alternating anoxic and aerobic conditions. In the aerobic conditions, ammonia present in the wastewater is converted to a nitrate (NO3 ) via nitrite (NO2 ). When the reactor is switched to anoxic conditions and the supply of oxygen by aeration ceases, denitriﬁcation takes place and NO3 is reduced to nitrogen gas. Raw wastewater is also added to this phase, thus supplying a readily bio-available carbon source to facilitate nitrogen removal. The switching of the operation is automated through an online measurement- based control system which monitors NO3eN and NH4eN concentrations in the reactors, in order to optimize nitrogen removal (Ronsen et al., 2006).

Four reactors having two basins each, with a total volume of 80,000 m3, operate at a retention time of approximately

24 h. The two basins alternate between aerobic/anoxic con- ditions and operate in a semi-batch manner. Each phase lasts between 0.5 and 2 h, depending on concentrations of ammonia and NO3 in the reactor (4). Efﬂuent from the aera- tion basins is sent to a two-stage sedimentation process to settle out any remaining phosphorus (5). Primary and sec- ondary sludge is pumped to four egg-shaped, mesophilic anaerobic digesters (6). Generated biogas is utilized for elec- tricity and heat consumption on site (7), Digested sludge is stored in an aerated ﬂow equalization pond (8) and then dewatered using a decanter centrifuge. The dewatered sludge is then dried by heat recovered from subsequent incineration processes and is sent to a ﬂuidized bed incinerator, the oper- ating temperature of which is approximately 950 C. Dew- atering, thermal drying, and sludge incineration take place in the same building (9). Flue gas from the incinerators is treated by an electrostatic precipitator, a bag ﬁlter with activated carbon and lime injection, quenchers, and scrubbers. Treated wastewater is used as cooling water for ﬂue gas treatment and the drying process, while ash from the electrostatic pre- cipitators and bag ﬁlters is deposited in an on-site disposal facility (10).

2.2. Quantiﬁcation of gas emissions

Gas emission rates were quantiﬁed through mobile mea- surement of the downwind plumes of target gases and a tracer gas (Galle et al., 2001; Scheutz et al., 2011; Mønster et al., in press). Acetylene (C2H2) was used as a tracer gas and released at a constant rate. By comparing the downwind plume concentrations of the target gas and the tracer gas, the real-time emission rate of the target gas can be determined using the following equation:

Etarget gas ¼ Qtracer Z plume end

where Etarget gas is the emission of the investigated gas in kg h 1; Qtracer is the known release of tracer gas in kg h 1; Ctarget gas and Ctracer are the measured downwind concen- trations in parts per billion (ppb), Ctarget gas background and Ctracer background are the background concentrations in ppb; and MWtarget gas and MWtracer are the molar weights of the methane and tracer gas. The measurements were conducted by driving through the downwind N2O, CH4, and C2H2 plumes multiple times. The plumes were integrated for each measurement sweep, giving a real-time, plant integrated emission rate for the duration of the plume traverse.

Two mobile measurement devices were used for the detection of atmospheric concentrations downwind from the sources. Both instruments were based on CRDS, an optical technology in which the direct measurement of infrared ab- sorption loss in a sample cell is used to quantify the mole fraction of the gas. One instrument was equipped with lasers, to detect CH4 and C2H2 (G2203, Picarro, Inc., Santa Clara, CA), and another to detect N2O/NH3/H2O (S/N JADS2001, Picarro,

Inc., Santa Clara, CA). Two separate lasers are used in these spectrometers e one to measure N2O and the other to mea- sure NH3 and H2O. Light from each laser, tuned to speciﬁc near-infrared absorption for the targeted analyte molecules, is directed sequentially into an optical resonator known as an ‘optical cavity’, which consists of a closed chamber with three highly reﬂective mirrors and serves as a compact ﬂow cell with a volume of less than 10 standard cm3 into which the sample gas is introduced. The ﬂow cell has an effective optical path length of 15e20 km, and this long path length allows for highly precise measurements (with ppb or even parts-per- trillion uncertainty, depending on the analyte gas), using compact and extremely reliable near-infrared laser sources. Gas temperature and pressure are controlled rigidly in these instruments ([Crosson,](#acknowledgments) [2008)](#acknowledgments), and this stability allows the in- strument (when properly calibrated to traceable reference standards) to deliver accurate measurements that need very infrequent calibrations relative to other N2O/NH3/H2O instru- mentation. A further description of the equipment is pre- sented in Mønster et al. (in press).

The instrument monitors and controls optical wavelength precisely, which delivers sub-picometer wavelength targeting on a microsecond timescale. Ring-down events are collected at a rate of about 200 ring-downs per second, while individual spectrograms consist of about 50e100 individual ring-downs (or 0.25e0.5 s), distributed across 10-20 spectral points around the peak. The overall measurement interval is about 1 s. The resulting spectrograms are analyzed using nonlinear spectral pattern recognition routines, and the outputs of these routines are converted into gas concentrations using linear conversion factors derived from calibrations using gravi- metric standards or other artifact standards.

A series of laboratory tests, performed to establish the basic performance of the analyzer, consisted of continuous measurements of prepared gas mixtures. The measured per- formance of the N2O/NH3/H2O analyzer is summarized in Table 1.N2O measurements were calibrated using a nominally ambient concentration mixture of N2O in synthetic air. The calibration was then compared using an instrument cali- brated with known standards of N2O, while the NH3 mea- surement was calibrated against a 25 ppm gravimetric standard. Cross-talk from water vapor, CO2, and CH4 was determined to be \<5 ppb N2O/% H2O, \<1 ppb N2O/100 ppm CO2, and \<1 ppb N2O/ppm CH4, respectively. Both instruments were connected to a GPS, which recorded the geographical location of each atmospheric concentration measurement with a positioning accuracy of 20 cm. Temperature, atmo- spheric pressure, and wind speed and direction were recorded

simultaneously by a mobile weather station. The air intake of the mobile sampling device was set above ground at 2 m. Initial emission screenings were conducted to identify the major sources of N2O and CH4 emissions and the background concentration of target gases. Measurements were taken both up- and downwind of the WWTP. Some localized measure- ments were performed inside the plant, by visiting each unit process described in Section 2.1. A plastic ﬂoating chamber (diameter: 20 cm, height: 25 cm) was also used to measure emissions from exposed aqueous surfaces such as aeration basins and clariﬁers.

Measurements were performed on nine separate occa- sions, from May 2012 through May 2013. Weather conditions and surface morphology affect how gases are diluted, so the measurement campaigns were scheduled for when the wind direction enabled downwind plume measurements of the main sources of fugitive N2O and CH4 emissions. Table 2 summarizes weather conditions during the individual mea- surement campaigns. In order to treat the entire AV WWTP as a point source, measurements were taken at 400e1200 m away from the AV WWTP. Due to the low background con- centration of C2H2 and high CRDS sensitivity, the use of tracer gas was minimal, ranging from 0.2 through 0.9 kg h 1. This release rate gave a downwind plume concentration of 2e30 ppb.

3\. Results and discussion

3.1. CH4 emissions

Plant-integrated CH4 emissions from AV WWTP measured between 4.99 and 92.3 kg h 1, depending on the sampling day (Table 2), while observations of high emissions concentrated around the spring months. Initial screenings on and around the WWTP showed CH4 emissions from a number of sources. CH4 plumes were identiﬁed downwind of the facility, and quantiﬁcation measurements were taken at a minimum of 1200 m away, depending on the wind direction and available roads, to cover the entire plant as a single point source of emissions. During the quantiﬁcation of CH4 emissions, tracer gas was released at the sludge handling area, thus providing comparable CH4 and tracer gas plumes downwind from the WWTP (see Fig. 2). If other CH4 emission sources have had relative signiﬁcance (e.g. aeration tanks or primary/secondary clariﬁers), an extension of the CH4 plume would have been seen towards the east in Fig. 2.

AV WWTP's CH4 plume showed large ﬂuctuations over a short period, punctuated by a spike in emissions of around 90e120 kg h 1. Fig. 3 shows the time series for the emissions on May 14th, 2013, when this trend is most profoundly pre- sented. Initial screenings of CH4 from each unit's processes revealed that the most signiﬁcant CH4 emissions emanated from areas around the anaerobic digesters, indicated as (6) in Fig. 1. This was also conﬁrmed with a good match obtained between the tracer gas plume and the CH4 plume, when tracer gas was placed next to the anaerobic digesters, as shown in Fig. 2. The upper part of Fig. 2 presents the relative atmo- spheric concentration of CH4 and C2H2 above background concentration measured on March 31st. Background

(2011) used isotopomer analysis and proved that N2O production also takes place in the anoxic tank, where nitrite is reduced via denitriﬁcation. In our study, ﬂuctuations in N2O emissions were observed both between measurement campaigns (Table

2. and within individual measurement campaigns (Fig. 5). However, no clear relationship was established between short-term changes in N2O emission and the mode of opera- tion since the four BioDeNitro reactors at the AV WWTP were not operating in sync. Uncoordinated aeration cycle for each basin masks the emission pattern and poses limitations in correlating of N2O emission rates and operational parameters, since the emissions from individual basins could not be distinguished by the tracer dilution method.

The production of N2O is inﬂuenced by many factors. Some could be design parameters such as high internal recycle rates and low design efﬂuent N concentrations, but many are operational parameters at the WWTPs (Foley et al., 2010; Lotito et al., 2012). Elevated N2O emissions have been recorded when the temperature of wastewater falls below 15 C (Daelman et al., 2013b). At AV WWTP, the water temperature ranged between 11.3 and 14.9 C(Table 3), while the highest emissions were observed on the day (March 31st 2013, Table 2 with the lowest water temperature (Table 3). Besides water tempera- ture, low dissolved oxygen (DO) levels, high N loads into the reactor, high NO2 concentrations, and low COD/N ratios dur- ing the denitriﬁcation process are listed by [Aboobakar](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.](#acknowledgments) [(2013)](#acknowledgments) and Kampschreur et al. (2009) as major contributors to elevated N2O generation.

At the AV WWTP, the DO level remained at 1.0e2.0 mg L 1. The length of aeration is controlled by in-line measurement of NHþ4 and NO3 concentrations in the aeration basins. When these concentrations drop to the predeﬁned threshold, the aeration regime changes automatically. No record for NO2 was available at the study site.

Throughout each measurement campaign, the wastewater load, and rate of internal recycling remained stable. The level of NHþ4 was not properly recorded due to the malfunction of an in-line monitoring device on March 31st, 2013. At the same day, elevated NO3 levels were found in reactors: NO3 levels

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 5 e N2O emissions from AV WWTP on March 31st, 2013.

ranged from 1.8 to 6.6 mg L 1 over aeration cycles, while NO3 levels varied between 0.6 and 3.6 mg L 1 during other days. During the period with elevated NO3 levels, the highest N2O emissions were measured (Table 2). The correlation between elevated NO2 in solution and N2O emissions is well- documented (Kampschreur et al., 2009; Desloover et al., 2012; Aboobakar et al., 2013) but also found the levated NO3 concentrations in reactors were also occur along with higher N2O emissions in previous studies (Su¨ mer et al., 1995; Sun et al., 2013).

Sufﬁcient reduction of NHþ4 and accumulation of NO3 found on March 31st indicates that the ABO and NOB were properly functioning but that the activity of denitriﬁers was inhibited, possibly due to the over aeration. AOB, NOB and a range of other microbes contribute to the N turnover pathway to N2O but only denitriﬁers can reduce N2O to N2 (Schreiber et al., 2012), which could explain the higher emission of N2O. It is clear that on March 31st, conditions were favorable for the higher emission of N2O (i.e. low water temperature, NO3 accumulation). Hence, the actual factor contributing to elevated emissions could not be singled out. Further research on the relationship between the optimization of biological nitrogen removal processes and N2O emissions is anticipated. Quantifying N2O levels presents challenges, not only due to its low emission rate but also to the nature of its emission. In comparison to CH4, N2O was emitted from a larger surface area, which implies that a greater measuring distance is required before the emission area can be considered a point source. As measuring distance increases the dilution of the emitted gases also increases, posing a challenge for analytical sensitivity. Detection limits in measurements were typically 0.3e0.4 kg h 1 at distances of 400e600 m, but these could vary through atmospheric turbulence caused by wind, typography, and incoming solar radiation.

The present study shows that it is possible to quantify N2O emissions from a WWTP employing a biological nitrogen removal process. It i reported that the plants without biolog- ical nitrogen removal process are likely to have lower N2O emission rate (Law et al., 2012). In order to expand the mea- surement campaign to plants without these speciﬁc pro- cesses, and provide a better scope for N2O emissions from wastewater treatment process, improvements in CRDS and emission data processing would be required.

3.3. Emission factors

The structural and operational losses of CH4 were calculated by taking the ratio between the amount of CH4 emitted and the sum CH4 emitted and utilized. The loss of CH4 quantiﬁed in the present study was found to be 2.1e4.4% of the gas generated when the plant was operating in steady conditions, but much higher losses were observed during periods of operational difﬁculties (32.7% of CH4 generation). Under the IPCC guideline, any loss of CH4 into the atmo- sphere is accounted for indirectly. The estimation of CH4 released from wastewater treatment facilities follows the general equation: (Equation (2))

CH4 emissions ¼ B$MCF$ðTOW SÞ R (2)

Table 3 e Operational parameters for the secondary treatment Date Inﬂuent ﬂow Sludge Water

a The range is given to capture the variation in peak concentration over b The in-line monitoring device failed to perform properly.

where B ¼ maximum CH4-producing capacity (0.6 kg CH4/kg BOD), MCF ¼ CH4 correction factor (fraction), TOW ¼ total organics in wastewater (kg BOD), S ¼ total organic carbon removed as sludge in an inventory year (kg BOD), and R ¼ amount of CH4 recovered in an inventory year (kg CH4). Based on operational data, the average daily load of BOD was 142,000 kg d 1 and the average daily CH4 utilisation rate was 6013 kg d 1. The removal of organic carbon as digested sludge stood at 20.1%, based on a material ﬂow analysis study con- ducted at the same plant (Yoshida et al., in press), while MCF was set at 0.9, a mid-range point for the values suggested by the guideline (0.8e1.0), which would give an emission rate of

5.1 kg CH4 h 1 or a leakage rate of 2.0%. The UNFCCC clean development mechanism (CDM) protocol states that for the anaerobic digestion of organic waste, 2.8% of the generated biogas is lost via physical leakage, unless a lower rate can be demonstrated ([CDM,](#acknowledgments) [2012)](#acknowledgments).

The loss of biogas recorded in the present study was consistent with recent measurement campaigns conducted at agricultural anaerobic digesters: Leakage rates of 1.7e5.2% of the produced biogas (Flesch et al., 2011) and of 0.3e2.6% (Liebetrau et al., 2013) have been reported. Both studies state that roughly 10% of the generated CH4 was emitted during ﬂaring and venting periods (Flesch et al., 2011) and from the open storage of digestate (Liebetrau et al., 2013).

Under the IPCC guideline, N2O emissions associated with WWTPs are calculated on two levels: N2O emissions from WWTPs and elevated N2O caused by the introduction of reactive N into the surrounding environment as a result of discharging treated wastewater. Emissions from WWTPs are estimated by the following Equation (3):

N2O emissions ¼ P\*Fadd\*EFplant (3)

where P ¼ service population, Fadd ¼ fraction of industrial and commercial co-discharge of N, and EFplant ¼ emission factor of the WWTP (g N2O person 1 yr 1). The suggested value in 2006's IPCC guideline for the EFplant factor was 3.2 g N2O person 1 yr 1, with a range of 2.0e8.0. The same guideline cites annual per capita protein consumption as 111 kg person 1 yr 1 and the proportion of nitrogen in protein as 0.16, while the factor for non-consumed protein added to waste- water is 1.1. If emission factors were calculated based on these assumptions, the EFplant factor, suggested by the guideline, could be translated to 0.0046e0.11% of N in inﬂuent emitted as N2O. This number is based on measurements conducted at a plant, which was not equipped with a biological nitrogen

process related to N2O emissions. Maximum dissolved Maximum ammonia Maximum

removal process ([Czepiel](#acknowledgments) [et](#acknowledgments) [al.,](#acknowledgments) [1995)](#acknowledgments). Based on previous studies, higher N2O emissions are expected from WWTPs equipped with a biological nitrogen removal process (Su¨ mer et al., 1995; Benckiser et al., 1996; Sommer et al., 1998; Kampschreur et al., 2009; Ahn et al., 2010; Townsend-Small et al., 2011; Ren et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2013). When normal- ized by the average daily N loading rate (3.67 MgeN d 1 with an 83.2% N removal rate through a wastewater treatment process), emissions factors in the present study ranged from

0.15 (detection limit) through 4.27% of N in inﬂuent water. This is higher than the value used by the IPCC 2006 guideline, but it is still within the range of the values reported by previous studies ([Fig.](#acknowledgments) [6)](#acknowledgments).

3.4. Environmental assessment

In order to put the emission factors obtained from the mea- surement campaigns in perspective, a detailed lifecycle assessment of the AV WWTP was conducted, including the GHG embedded in the electricity and treatment chemicals. All the GHG emissions were normalized to global warming po- tential (kg CO2-eq) by following the IPCC 2007 characterization method (Yoshida et al., 2014). Provisioning of electricity to the wastewater treatment process was found to be the biggest contributor of global warming (GW) from the plant, but the on- site GHG emission also occupied a major portion of GW impact: 23.7% of the GW potential was fromN2O emissions and 6.9% from CH4 at normal plant operation conditions. N2O emissions alone were enough to cancel out the GW savings from avoided production of electricity due to biogas utilization. Furthermore, the overall GW impact was found very sensitive to the rate of N2O and CH4 emissions. During periods of elevated N2O and CH4 emissions, the GW impact of the plant increased by 110 and 56%, respectively, makingon-site GHG emissions the biggest contributor to GWP from the operation of WWTP. The leakage of biogas from anaerobic digestion is associ- ated with the release of H2S and NH3, both of which cause odor problems and induce terrestrial acidiﬁcation and eutrophica- tion. Tracer dilution methods provided the means to perform a plant-integrated GHG measurement for WWTPs. As both N2O and CH4 emissions have a profound effect on determining the environmental performance of WWTPs, further accumu- lation of knowledge on the cause of elevated emissions and mitigation measures is anticipated.

In formulating mitigation strategies, it should be noted that the tracer dilution method only captures the amount of
